newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks rally expected to continue and broaden.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks rally expected to continue and broaden.

text.p: The U.S. stock market rally that has taken market indicators to record levels is likely to keep going through the end of the year, although some traders say a nice Christmas present would be seeing some of the smaller issues hop on the bandwagon.
"A broadening of the advance will be a healthy thing," said a Wall Street trader who declined to be identified.

He said some of the big name stocks that have been the best performers in the rally are at such lofty heights that individual issues could take a severe pounding in the event of some unforeseen disappointment.

"What we have had has been a narrowing of leadership in the market," said Marion Schultheis, vice president and senior portfoliio manager at IDS Equity Advisors. She compared it to the 1970-72 period when most of the acton and most of the talk on Wall Street was focused on a select group popularly known as the "nifty-fifty."

Today's list of favorites, she said, is populated by companies that analysts believe can deliver dependable earnings growth even if the economy slows down. In fact most of the companies have a global reach so that overseas business can compensate for any slack in the U.S. economy.

Schultheis and other analysts said while there are some differences of opinion about which stocks are in the new, bigger "nifty-fifty," typical candidates are General Electric Co, International Business Machines Corp Corp, Intel Corp, Microsoft Corp and Compaq Computer Corp.
Other candidates come from the health care area.
"I think between now and the end of the year money will still flow into those names," Schultheis said.
Trude Latimer, an independent analyst based in Charlottesville, Va., agreed that the smaller issues have taken a back seat.

"For months now, it's been a small handful of stocks that have been doing the whole thing," Latimer said. "When low-priced stocks are moving they're moving for two days. We have not had a real move in stocks selling below $10 unless it's a specific stock and a particularly hot area."

Latimer and others say that many individual investors who ordinarily might consider buying a low-priced, small capitaliztion stock now do their investing by buying a hot mutual fund. But the fund manager considers these lower-priced stocks too illiquid to buy.

According to Schultheis one scenario that could unfold in January is a move into cyclical stocks such as papers and luminums. But she said this could be a "false rally" and fund managers will have a tough time deciding whether to cut exposure in the current "nifty fifty" group and jump into the cyclicals, or just stand pat.

As for the longer-term outlook, Schultheis thinks "fundamentals for the market are pretty positive for 12-to-18 months. "Hight valuations by themselves don't mean that stocks will go down." If there is a risk in the market, she said, it is "risk the economy is stronger than people are anticipating rather than weaker."
Schultheis and others agreed that the high valuations for the current "nifty-fifty" group cannot be compared to the atmospheric valuations accorded the favored few in the early 1970's.

The trader who preferred to be anonymous noted with some irony that the 1970's "nifty fifty" group included some well-known names that went on to disappoint investors later on including Avon Products Inc, Xerox Corp and Polaroid Corp. "It took Avon 10 years to recuperate after the bubble burst," he said.
The Dow industrials closed Wednesday, before the Thanksgiving day break, at 6499. The industrials are up about 27 percent since the beginning of the year.
